lessons.title: Recruiting and Hiring Beauty Professionals
lessons.body: To find good stylists, braiders, or barbers, you need to look in the right places. Start by asking your current staff for referralsâoffer them a bonus of 500 to 1,000 shillings or naira if their friend stays for three months. Post on local WhatsApp groups, Facebook marketplace, and notice boards at beauty schools. When you get applicants, give them a practical test. Ask them to braid a mannequin or do a quick weave in 30 minutes. Watch how they handle tools and talk to a pretend client. Check references by calling their last employer. Ask: 'Did they show up on time? How did they treat clients?' For pay, start with a base salary plus commission. For example, in Kenya, a junior stylist might get 15,000 KES base plus 10% of services they perform. In Nigeria, 40,000 NGN base plus 15% commission. Always have a written contract stating hours, pay, and notice period. During the interview, ask situational questions: 'A client is unhappy with her hair. What do you do?' Listen for problem-solving and respect. Don't hire someone just because they are your relativeâhire for skill and attitude. A bad hire costs you clients and money. A good hire brings in more business. Take your time, even if you are short-staffed. It is better to wait than to hire someone who will chase away your customers.

lessons.title: Training and Onboarding New Staff
lessons.body: When a new person joins your salon, the first week sets the tone. Don't just throw them on the floor. Start with a paid orientation day. Show them around: where the towels are kept, how to mix relaxer safely, how to use the booking book or app like Fresha or Salonist. Give them a checklist of 10 tasks to learn in the first week, like sanitizing combs, shampooing, and greeting clients. Pair them with a senior stylist for two weeks. The senior shows them your salon's way of doing thingsâhow you part hair, how you apply gel, how you talk to clients. Pay the senior a small training bonus, maybe 2,000 KES or 5,000 NGN per week. Hold a 15-minute meeting every morning to go over the day's appointments and any new products. After two weeks, do a skills check: can they do a basic wash and blow-dry without help? If not, give more practice time. Also train them on customer service: how to answer the phone, how to handle a client who is late, how to offer a drink. Use role-play. One person acts as an angry client, the other practices staying calm. Document your training so every new hire gets the same start. This saves you time and builds a consistent team.

lessons.title: Motivating and Retaining Employees
lessons.body: Good stylists leave when they feel stuck or underpaid. To keep them, you need to motivate them beyond just salary. First, pay fairly and on time. If you promise commission on a busy Saturday, pay it that same week. Late pay kills trust. Second, offer small perks: a free lunch on Saturdays, a birthday cake, or a bonus of 1,000 KES when they get a 5-star review from a client. Third, give them a clear path to grow. For example, a junior braider can become a senior braider after six months if they pass a skill test, with a 20% pay raise. Fourth, involve them in decisions. Ask: 'Which new hair product should we stock?' or 'How can we make the salon run smoother?' When people feel heard, they stay. Fifth, recognise good work publicly. At the end of the week, say: 'Grace did an amazing job on that bridal hairâeveryone clap for her.' That costs nothing but means a lot. Also, watch for burnout. If someone works six days a week, give them a extra day off after a busy season. Finally, be flexible. If a stylist has a family emergency, let them swap shifts. When you treat staff like family, they treat your salon like their own. Turnover drops, and clients notice a happy team.

lessons.title: Conflict Resolution and Team Communication
lessons.body: In any salon, people will argue. Maybe two stylists want the same client, or someone left the sterilizer dirty. Don't ignore itâit grows. When conflict happens, pull the people aside separately first. Ask each: 'What happened? How did it make you feel?' Listen without taking sides. Then bring them together and say: 'We are a team. Let's find a solution.' For example, if two braiders fight over a walk-in client, set a rule: clients go to whoever is next on the rotation list. Write it on a whiteboard. If someone leaves a mess, make a cleaning roster with names and times. Check it every evening. For bigger issues, like stealing or constant lateness, have a private meeting. Use 'I' statements: 'I feel frustrated when you arrive 30 minutes late because I have to cover your clients.' Then agree on a consequence: if late again, no commission for that day. Also, hold a 20-minute team meeting every Monday. Go around the room: each person says one thing that went well and one thing that needs fixing. No blaming. Use a talking stick or a small objectâonly the person holding it speaks. This stops interruptions. If two people still can't work together, change their shifts so they don't overlap. Your job is to keep the salon peaceful so clients feel calm.

lessons.title: Performance Reviews and Goal Setting
lessons.body: A performance review is not a punishment. It is a check-in to help your staff grow. Do a formal review every three months. Sit down with each employee for 20 minutes. Use a simple form with three columns: 'What you do well', 'What needs improvement', 'Goals for next quarter'. Start with praise. For example: 'You are excellent at cornrowsâclients ask for you.' Then discuss one or two areas to improve. Maybe they need to be faster at shampooing, or they need to upsell hair products. Set a specific, measurable goal. Not 'be better at sales', but 'sell 10 bottles of leave-in conditioner next month'. Write it down. Agree on how you will help: maybe a short training or a script to practice. Also, let them set a personal goal, like 'learn to do eyelash extensions by June'. You pay for a course if they pass. After the review, follow up every two weeks with a quick 'How is that goal going?' If they meet it, give a reward: 2,000 KES bonus or a half-day off. If they don't, ask what got in the way. Maybe they need more practice. Never compare one employee to another in the review. Compare them to their own past performance. This makes them feel safe and motivated. Keep a copy of the review in a locked file. It protects you if you later need to let someone go.

lessons.title: Creating a Positive Workplace Culture
lessons.body: Culture is how your salon feels when you walk in. A positive culture makes staff want to come to work and clients want to stay. Start with your own behaviour. If you are always late, they will be too. If you gossip, they will gossip. Be the example. Greet everyone by name every morning. Say 'please' and 'thank you'. When a client complains, don't shout at the stylist in front of others. Take them to the back and talk quietly. Create small rituals: a 5-minute dance party before opening on Saturdays, or a shared lunch on the last Friday of the month. Celebrate wins: if the salon hits its monthly target, order pizza or give a 500 KES bonus to each person. Also, make the physical space pleasant. Play soft music, keep mirrors clean, have a kettle for tea. A dirty, tense salon drives away both staff and clients. Encourage staff to suggest improvements. Put a suggestion box (a simple notebook) in the back. Read it weekly and act on good ideas. When someone makes a mistake, focus on the fix, not the blame. Ask: 'What can we learn?' Finally, protect your team from abusive clients. If a client yells at a stylist, you step in and say, 'We treat everyone with respect here.' Your staff will remember that. A positive culture is your best recruitment and retention tool.

quiz.q: What is a good way to find new stylists for your salon?
options: B) Ask current staff for referrals and offer a bonus
C) Post on international job boards
D) Wait for people to walk in
quiz.explanation: Referrals from current staff often bring in reliable candidates, and a bonus motivates them to help.

quiz.q: During a practical test for a braider, what should you ask them to do?
options: B) Braid a mannequin in 30 minutes
quiz.explanation: A timed practical test shows their actual skill and speed.

quiz.q: What should be included in a written contract for a new hire?
options: B) Hours, pay, and notice period
quiz.explanation: A contract must clearly state working conditions to avoid disputes.

quiz.q: Why is it important to call references before hiring?
options: B) To check punctuality and client treatment
C) To ask for free products
D) To invite them to a party
quiz.explanation: References give insight into past behaviour and work ethic.

quiz.q: What is a fair starting pay structure for a junior stylist?
options: C) No pay for first month
quiz.explanation: Base plus commission provides security and motivation.

quiz.q: What should you do on a new hire's first day?
options: B) Give a paid orientation and tour
D) Ask them to bring clients
quiz.explanation: Orientation helps them learn the salon and feel welcome.

quiz.q: How long should a senior stylist mentor a new hire?
quiz.explanation: Two weeks of close mentoring builds confidence and consistency.

quiz.q: What is a good way to train customer service?
options: B) Role-play with an angry client
quiz.explanation: Role-play lets staff practice handling real situations safely.

quiz.q: Why should you document your training process?
options: B) To ensure every new hire gets the same start
quiz.explanation: Documentation ensures consistency and saves time.

quiz.q: What is a simple daily meeting to align the team?
quiz.explanation: Short daily huddles keep everyone focused and informed.

quiz.q: What kills trust among staff?
options: B) Late pay and broken promises
quiz.explanation: Late pay and broken promises make staff feel disrespected.

quiz.q: What is a low-cost way to motivate employees?
options: B) Public recognition and small perks
quiz.explanation: Recognition and small perks cost little but boost morale.

quiz.q: How can you give a clear path to growth?
options: A) Keep everyone at same level
B) Promote based on skill tests and time
quiz.explanation: A clear promotion path motivates staff to stay and improve.

quiz.q: What should you do if a stylist is burned out?
options: B) Give extra day off after busy season
quiz.explanation: Rest prevents burnout and keeps productivity high.

quiz.q: Why is flexibility important for retention?
options: A) It lets staff handle emergencies
C) It shows you don't care
quiz.explanation: Flexibility shows you value staff well-being, which builds loyalty.

quiz.q: What is the first step in resolving a conflict between two stylists?
quiz.explanation: Separate talks let you hear both sides without bias.

quiz.q: How can you fairly assign walk-in clients?
options: A) First come, first served by stylist
quiz.explanation: A rotation list ensures fairness and reduces arguments.

quiz.q: What is a good tool for weekly team meetings?
quiz.explanation: A talking stick ensures only one person speaks at a time.

quiz.q: What should you do if two staff members still can't work together?
options: A) Force them to work together
B) Change their shifts so they don't overlap
quiz.explanation: Separating shifts reduces tension and keeps the salon peaceful.

quiz.q: How often should you hold formal performance reviews?
quiz.explanation: Quarterly reviews give regular feedback and goal setting.

quiz.q: What is a specific, measurable goal for a stylist?
options: B) Sell 10 bottles of leave-in conditioner next month
quiz.explanation: Specific numbers make goals clear and trackable.

quiz.q: What should you do if an employee meets their goal?
options: B) Give a reward like a bonus
quiz.explanation: Rewarding success reinforces positive behaviour.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid comparing one employee to another in a review?
options: A) It makes them feel safe and motivated
quiz.explanation: Comparisons create jealousy and lower morale.

quiz.q: What should you keep in a locked file?
quiz.explanation: Keeping reviews protects you if you need to let someone go.

quiz.q: What is the best way to create a positive culture?
options: A) Be a good example yourself
quiz.explanation: Leaders set the tone; your behaviour sets the standard.

quiz.q: What is a small ritual that builds team spirit?
quiz.explanation: Fun rituals create bonding and reduce stress.

quiz.q: How should you handle a client who yells at a stylist?
options: B) Step in and defend your staff
quiz.explanation: Protecting your team shows respect and builds loyalty.

quiz.q: What is a simple way to gather staff ideas?
quiz.explanation: A suggestion notebook gives staff a voice and improves the salon.

quiz.q: What should you do when an employee makes a mistake?
options: A) Focus on the fix, not blame
quiz.explanation: Focusing on solutions helps learning and keeps morale high.

quiz.q: Why is a clean, pleasant physical space important?
options: A) It attracts staff and clients
quiz.explanation: A clean, welcoming environment makes people want to stay.
